title: The Danish Radio Big Band and state-funded jazz
summary: He praises the radio big band with strings and woodwind doublers, Niels-Henning bassist and Thad Jones as leader; government radio pays, and Denmark has ninety jazz clubs.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Oh - I work as much as I like in Denmark; as I said before, it's the only place where I've ever been where I really had to turn down work. You know--they've got probably one of the best big bands in Europe that works through the radio -- they call it the radio big band -- they use four trombones, five trumpets; they use six saxophones--
Oh - it's as big as that -- and

they even use strings; they use French horns and their trombone section - they use bass trombone and three regular trombones and every guy in that band doubles on flutes and clarinets and all the woodwinds; . they use sometimes two pianos and they have Niels-Henning which is probably one of the greatest bass players in the world, considered such and, uh, now I went to hear them on play on many occasions and I want to tell you, they are fantastic. They're as good as any big band that I've ever heard in America. They're just fantastic readers and they're all-- their trumpet players are all good for the type of music that's modern today. They can hit those high ones and they really know how to do it. And, now, they've got Thad Jones - now, Thad Jones went over there - did a tour with these guys and now he has a permanent position--
He broke up with Mel Lewis - everybody seems to know--
Yes but that was a long time ago.

But,now, here he is now living in Denmark; he bought himself a home and he runs that band and, so, they do lots of concerts over the air in the concert halls, which is broadcasted and they do all the main television work - you know - like if they're backing something big - Thad Jones and the Big Band behind it and, of course, it's such a small country, I wonder sometimes how they can pay such a big band - you know -it's really a
huge band. But, working for the radio or television in Denmark, you're working for the Government.
Well, that explains how they pay them.

That's right and, apparently, these guys make enough; they don't work that steadily all the time, you know, but they're working three, or four times a week and the rest of the time they're working for the radio and the television. So, that gives you a pretty good picture of what's happening in Denmark--

--and there seems to be more and more interest every year that I've been there. It's growing and growing and they're adding a jazz club here and there and there's ninety (90) jazz clubs already in Denmark; if you played 90 jazz clubs - if you played one every-- just make the rounds, you could work steadily the rest of your life-- just keep going around and around, but it's very hard to do that. Now, in Switzerland-- I said Switzerland-- the second time I went to Switzerland, of course, I did a Swiss Tour about 20 years ago; I did that for Joe Glaser's office and it was a cultural tour and I toured with a band then called the " Dark Town Strutters"
